content: The Children’s Oncology Group (COG) risk stratification system is utilized to determine the appropriate management protocol for neuroblastoma patients. For low-risk neuroblastoma patients, management typically involves either observation or surgical resection of the tumor. Observation is considered safe for low-risk patients younger than six months of age, even without obtaining a definitive histologic diagnosis or performing surgical intervention. This approach avoids potential surgical complications, as most neuroblastomas in this age group demonstrate spontaneous regression. Radiotherapy is generally not recommended for low-risk neuroblastoma patients. Chemotherapy is indicated in specific scenarios, such as: Stage 1 or Stage 2 tumors with MYCN amplification. Patients older than 18 months with Stage 2B tumors and unfavorable histology. Symptomatic patients experiencing spinal cord compression, respiratory compromise, or hepatic infiltration. Recommended chemotherapeutic agents for low-risk neuroblastoma include carboplatin, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and etoposide. For intermediate-risk neuroblastoma patients, management often involves neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by definitive surgical resection. Observation is not generally recommended for intermediate-risk patients. Radiotherapy may be indicated for life-threatening symptomatic neuroblastomas that are refractory to chemotherapy and/or surgery, or for rapidly progressing neuroblastomas. Chemotherapy is effective in treating intermediate-risk neuroblastoma. Patients with favorable histology are typically managed with four cycles of chemotherapy following surgery. Patients with unfavorable histology are managed with eight cycles of chemotherapy following surgery. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy may be employed to facilitate partial resection of previously unresectable tumors. Recommended chemotherapeutic agents for intermediate-risk neuroblastoma include carboplatin, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and etoposide. For high-risk neuroblastoma patients, a multimodal approach is employed, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy. Observation is not recommended for high-risk patients. Radiation therapy is used to consolidate local control after surgical resection. Chemotherapy for high-risk neuroblastoma is divided into three phases: Induction therapy: Chemotherapeutic regimens may include cisplatin, etoposide, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and topotecan. Consolidation therapy: This phase involves high-dose chemotherapy administered in tandem with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Maintenance therapy: Agents such as isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) are administered following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation to improve survival outcomes. This comprehensive approach ensures that treatment is tailored to the patient’s risk category, optimizing outcomes while minimizing unnecessary interventions.
